lines.text: Currency and payment systems have evolved dramatically, from ancient barter to digital wallets. The British pound sterling (£) — the world's oldest currency still in use — is divided into 100 pence. Coins come in denominations of 1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, £1, and £2. Banknotes are issued in £5, £10, £20, and £50 denominations, now made from polymer rather than paper. Payment methods have diversified enormously: cash was once dominant, but debit cards, credit cards, contactless payments, and mobile payments (Apple Pay, Google Pay) have taken over. The UK is one of the most cashless societies globally — many businesses no longer accept cash at all. Online payments use platforms like PayPal, bank transfers, and buy-now-pay-later services. Cryptocurrency — digital currencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum — represents a new frontier, though it remains volatile and not widely accepted for everyday transactions. Exchange rates fluctuate constantly, affecting international trade and travel. The foreign exchange market (forex) is the world's largest financial market. When travelling, people exchange currency at bureaux de change, banks, or airports. Understanding terms like exchange rate, commission, spread, and conversion fee helps avoid poor deals. Tipping culture varies: in British restaurants, 10-15% is customary (often added as a service charge); in taxis and hairdressers, rounding up is common. The shift from physical to digital currency raises important questions about privacy, accessibility, and financial inclusion.

lines.text: British English has colourful money slang: 'quid' (£1), 'fiver' (£5), 'tenner' (£10), 'grand' (£1,000), 'bob' (old shilling, now informal). Cockney rhyming slang adds: 'bread' (bread and honey = money), 'monkey' (£500), 'pony' (£25).

lines.text: British dining etiquette around bill-splitting is nuanced. 'Shall we split it?' is standard among friends. 'Going Dutch' is the idiom. Increasingly, apps like Splitwise handle group payments. Arguing over who pays is considered awkward.

lines.text: The UK's rapid move to cashless has sparked debate. Campaign groups argue cash protects vulnerable people — the elderly, those without bank accounts, and people in rural areas with poor internet. 'Access to cash' has become a political issue.

lines.text: British tipping is less obligatory than American. 10-15% in restaurants is standard (often auto-added as 'service charge'). Tipping taxi drivers, hairdressers, and hotel staff is appreciated but not expected. 'Keep the change' is a common casual tip.
